name: Mitral valve
func: A two-leaflet door between the left atrium and left ventricle. It opens to let oxygen-rich blood fill the ventricle and slams shut when the ventricle squeezes, so blood can't leak backward into the lungs.

levels.kid:
Inside your heart there are little doors that only open one way. The **mitral valve** is the door between the top-left room and the bottom-left room.

When blood comes back from your lungs full of fresh air, the door swings open and the blood pours down into the big pumping room. Then the pumping room squeezes, and — snap! — the door shuts tight so no blood can go backward.

The mitral valve has two flaps, and tiny strings hold them so they don't flip the wrong way, like the strings on a parachute. When a doctor listens to your heart, the "lub" sound is partly this door closing.
levels.hs:
The **mitral valve** (also called the **bicuspid** or **left atrioventricular valve**) sits between the **left atrium** and the **left ventricle**. It is the only heart valve with **two leaflets**: a large **anterior** leaflet and a smaller, longer-based **posterior** leaflet. It lies deep and toward the back of the heart, behind and to the left of the aortic valve, which sits right next to it.

The leaflets are attached by thin cords called **chordae tendineae** to two **papillary muscles** in the ventricle wall. When the ventricle contracts, the papillary muscles tighten the cords so the leaflets meet but don't flip back into the atrium (**prolapse**).

The mitral valve opens in **diastole** (filling) and closes at the start of **systole**. Its closing, together with the tricuspid's, makes the **first heart sound (S1)**, the "lub".

Its name comes from a bishop's hat, the **mitre**, which its two flaps resemble. Doctors listen to it best at the heart's **apex**.
levels.college:
The mitral apparatus has six parts: the **annulus**, two **leaflets**, the **commissures** (anterolateral and posteromedial), the **chordae tendineae**, the **papillary muscles** and the adjacent **LV wall**. Disease of any part can cause leakage.

The **annulus** is saddle-shaped (D-shaped in surgeons' views) and dynamic, shrinking and folding during systole to help the leaflets meet. The **anterior leaflet** is in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve (the **aortomitral curtain**) and is bordered by the left and non-coronary aortic cusps. Surgeons divide each leaflet into three scallops: **A1–A3** and **P1–P3** (Carpentier nomenclature).

Relations matter surgically: the **circumflex artery** runs in the groove close to the posterior annulus, the **coronary sinus** lies nearby, and the **AV node** sits near the posteromedial commissure. All can be injured during valve surgery.

Chordae come from both papillary muscles to both leaflets. The **posteromedial papillary muscle** usually has a single blood supply (from the posterior descending artery), so it ruptures more often after an inferior MI than the dual-supplied anterolateral one.

Normal mitral valve area is about 4–6 cm². On auscultation the valve is heard best at the apex, and its murmurs radiate toward the **left axilla**.
levels.phd:
Mitral leaflets are layered: the **atrialis** (elastin-rich, on the atrial side), the **spongiosa** (proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans that absorb shock), and the **fibrosa** (dense collagen, ventricular side, carrying load). They are covered by **valvular endothelial cells** and populated by **valvular interstitial cells (VICs)**, which maintain the matrix and can switch to an activated, myofibroblast-like state.

In **myxomatous degeneration** (the substrate of mitral valve prolapse), the spongiosa expands with proteoglycans, collagen becomes disorganized and the leaflets thicken and stretch. **TGF-β** signaling is a central driver; it is strikingly overactive in **Marfan syndrome** (fibrillin-1 mutations), where prolapse is common. Variants in genes such as **FLNA** and **DCHS1** cause familial prolapse, hinting at developmental roots.

**Rheumatic heart disease** works differently: antibodies against streptococcal antigens cross-react with valve proteins (**molecular mimicry**), causing inflammation, commissural fusion, chordal shortening and calcification, the classic "fish-mouth" stenotic valve.

Mechanically, mitral regurgitation is classified by the **Carpentier system**: type I (normal leaflet motion, e.g. annular dilation or perforation), type II (excessive motion, prolapse or chordal rupture), type IIIa (restricted in both phases, rheumatic) and type IIIb (restricted in systole, from a tethered ventricle after ischemia). **Functional (secondary) MR** is a ventricular disease: a dilated LV pulls the papillary muscles apart and tethers otherwise normal leaflets.
levels.expert:
**Mitral regurgitation (MR)** gives a **pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur** at the apex radiating to the **left axilla**. **Mitral stenosis (MS)** gives a **loud S1**, an **opening snap** and a low-pitched **mid-diastolic rumble** heard with the bell at the apex with the patient turned onto their left side. **Mitral valve prolapse** gives a **mid-systolic click** followed by a late systolic murmur; standing moves the click earlier.

MS raises left atrial pressure, causing atrial enlargement, **atrial fibrillation** and **left atrial thrombus**. That makes rheumatic MS with AF one of the highest-risk settings for **cardioembolic stroke**, often a large MCA territory infarct, which is why neurologists and neurosurgeons care about this valve.

Acute severe MR (from papillary muscle rupture after MI or chordal rupture) causes sudden **pulmonary edema** and shock and is a surgical emergency. **Infective endocarditis** on the mitral valve can throw septic emboli to the brain, causing infarcts, abscesses or **mycotic aneurysms**.

Imaging: **transthoracic echo** first; **transesophageal echo (TEE)** gives the best view because the esophagus lies right behind the left atrium. TEE is also how clinicians look for atrial thrombus.

Treatment in general terms: surgical **repair** is preferred over replacement for degenerative MR; **balloon valvotomy** for suitable rheumatic MS; **transcatheter edge-to-edge repair** (clipping the leaflets together) for high-risk patients; and anticoagulation when AF or a mechanical valve is present.

keyPoints: Between left atrium and left ventricle; the only two-leaflet valve
Anchored by chordae tendineae to two papillary muscles
Closure contributes to S1; heard best at the apex
MR: pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
MS: opening snap + diastolic rumble; causes AF and atrial clots → stroke

test.q: How many leaflets does the mitral valve have?
test.explain: It's bicuspid: anterior and posterior leaflets. The other three heart valves have three leaflets/cusps.

test.q: The thin cords tying the mitral leaflets to the papillary muscles are the ______.
test.explain: Chordae tendineae, tensioned by the papillary muscles, stop the leaflets prolapsing into the atrium in systole.

test.q: Mitral regurgitation's murmur classically radiates to the:
test.explain: MR is a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla; aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids.

test.q: Which papillary muscle ruptures more often after an MI, and why?
choices: Posteromedial, because it usually has a single blood supply
Anterolateral, because it has no chordae
Posteromedial, because it is in the right ventricle
test.explain: The posteromedial muscle usually relies on the posterior descending artery alone; the anterolateral gets LAD and circumflex blood.

test.q: Mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation greatly raises the risk of what brain event?
test.explain: A stagnant, enlarged left atrium forms clots that can embolize to the brain.
